title_en.value: Mandibular Veneers: Are They Really as Reliable as Maxillary Ones?

caption_en.value: The enamel of the mandibular incisors is thinner, so do mandibular veneers perform worse? A review of the 3-, 7- and 10-year reports of one study on extended veneers, and the role of exposed dentin.

body_en.value:
The labial enamel of the mandibular incisors is thinner than that of the maxillary incisors; this difference is particularly pronounced in the cervical region [4].

This difference matters clinically. Suppose both arches of a patient are to be treated with ceramic veneers. If reaching the same final shade needs a similar ceramic thickness, dentin is more likely to be exposed in the mandible, because we have less enamel to work with.

On the other hand, we know that dentin exposure can increase the likelihood of veneer complications [1][2][3]. So the initial expectation is that mandibular veneers would perform worse.

But does the clinical evidence confirm this expectation?

## One study; three reports at three time points

The 3-, 7- and 10-year articles we review below are not three independent studies; they are consecutive reports on one group of patients [1][2][3].

In this study, the veneers in both arches were placed by one dentist with a similar treatment protocol. Patients with bruxism were also excluded from the study. So the results should be interpreted in light of these conditions.

## Type of veneers; an important point in interpreting the results

The veneers used in this study were of the Extended type; that is, the ceramic did not cover only the labial surface, but passed over the incisal edge and extended onto the palatal or lingual surface.

In this design, the ceramic coverage could also extend into the proximal areas and, to correct a diastema or displaced teeth or to cover previous restorations, could involve a larger part of the tooth structure.

[[Image:01]]

*Figure 1. Veneer preparation principles (A) and the extended proximal design (B) [1]. Source: Rinke et al., 2013, Figure 1; reproduced with permission, as stated by the founder.*

[[Image:02]]

*Figure 2. Preparation of four extended veneers in the mandible (A) and the clinical situation at the five-year follow-up (B) [2]. Source: Rinke et al., 2018, Figure 2; reproduced with permission, as stated by the founder.*

For this reason, in terms of coverage, these restorations sit between a conventional veneer and a full crown.

The important point is that in both arches, dentin was exposed during preparation [2][3].

The researchers assessed the amount of exposed dentin after the final preparation and divided the veneers into two groups depending on whether less or more than 50 percent of the preparation surface involved dentin [1][2][3].

[[Image:03]]

*Figure 3. A: preparation with less than 50% exposed dentin, after etching with phosphoric acid. B: preparation with more than 50% exposed dentin in the maxilla [1]. Source: Rinke et al., 2013, Figure 2; reproduced with permission, as stated by the founder.*

## Results at three, seven and ten years

| Measure | 3 years | 7 years | 10 years |
|---|---|---|---|
| Survival of maxillary veneers | 94.2% | 95% | 91.9% |
| Survival of mandibular veneers | 96.7% | 91.2% | 91.7% |
| Success, maxilla | 91.5% | 82.1% | 74.7% |
| Success, mandible | 94.9% | 88% | 85.7% |
| Increased risk of needing an intervention when more than 50% of dentin is exposed | 10.6 times | 3.71 times | 2.98 times |

To interpret these numbers, we need to know the difference between the two measures:

Survival: the veneer is still in the patient's mouth, even if it has needed an intervention such as recementation during this time. A fracture that leads to replacing the veneer counts as a failure.

Success: a stricter criterion. The veneer has stayed in the mouth without needing any intervention.

In all three reports, no significant difference was seen in the survival of veneers in the two arches [1][2][3].

[[Image:04]]

*Figure 4. Survival probability by jaw in the ten-year report; black: maxilla, red: mandible, horizontal axis: months [3]. Source: Rinke et al., 2020, Figure 5; reproduced with permission, as stated by the founder.*

For success, the picture was somewhat different. The success rate of mandibular veneers was higher at all three time points, and this difference grew over time, so that in the ten-year report the difference came close to the threshold of statistical significance [1][2][3].

[[Image:05]]

*Figure 5. Success (intervention-free) probability by jaw in the ten-year report; black: maxilla, red: mandible [3]. Source: Rinke et al., 2020, Figure 8; reproduced with permission, as stated by the founder.*

So, contrary to the initial expectation, this study shows no evidence of poorer performance of mandibular veneers.

## Exposed dentin; the more important factor in predicting complications

One of the study's important findings was the relationship between the amount of exposed dentin and the need for intervention.

Veneers in which more than half of the preparation surface was in dentin needed intervention more often at all three time points. The most common intervention was recementation, and root canal treatment was also seen in all three reports [1][2][3].

That said, this difference did not necessarily mean lower veneer survival; that is, despite the greater need for intervention, no significant difference was observed in the likelihood of the veneers staying in place or being lost.

The timing of complications is also interesting.

In the group in which more than 50 percent of the preparation surface involved dentin, the first interventions started in the early months and continued in the following years.

In contrast, in the group with less exposed dentin, almost no problems were reported up to about five years, and complications appeared gradually in the later years [3].

[[Image:06]]

*Figure 6. Success probability by amount of exposed dentin in the ten-year report; black: 50% or less, red: more than 50% [3]. Source: Rinke et al., 2020, Figure 9; reproduced with permission, as stated by the founder.*

This pattern shows that the two groups differed not only in the number of complications but also in when they occurred.

Another point to note is the decrease in the risk ratio for needing intervention over time. This figure went from 10.6 times at three years to about 3 times at ten years [1][2][3].

This decrease does not mean that dentin becomes unimportant in the long term. In the early years, the low-dentin group was almost free of complications, and this made the risk ratio look very high. Over time, complications appeared in the low-dentin group too, and the gap between the two groups narrowed.

[[Image:07]]

*Figure 7. Success probability by amount of exposed dentin in the three-year report; black: less than 50%, red: more than 50%, horizontal axis: months [1]. Source: Rinke et al., 2013, Figure 6; reproduced with permission, as stated by the founder.*

Even so, their difference in success still remained by the end of ten years [3].

Clinically, one can take this to mean that problems related to bonding to dentin may manifest earlier, although this interpretation is our reading of the trend in the results, not a direct conclusion of the authors.

## Can we trust the superiority of mandibular veneers?

Despite the study's interesting results, there are several important limitations that should be considered.

1. The amount of exposed dentin is not given separately for each arch.

This is the most important limitation for answering our main question.

We know that the enamel of the mandibular incisors is thinner; but the study does not specify how much of the preparation surface of the maxillary and mandibular veneers actually involved dentin.

So we cannot check whether the thinner enamel of the mandible actually led to more dentin exposure. As a result, the reason for the similar or even better performance of the mandibular veneers remains unclear.

2. Follow-up of the two arches was not exactly the same.

More mandibular veneers dropped out of follow-up during the study, and their follow-up time was also shorter overall [1][2][3].

This matters, because the likelihood of failure and of needing intervention increases over time. So the possibility that this difference in follow-up had an effect cannot be ignored.

3. Some numbers are not consistent between the reports.

For example, the survival of mandibular veneers is reported slightly higher in the ten-year report than in the seven-year report, whereas in a fixed group survival should not increase over time [2][3].

There are also several other inconsistencies in the three-year report [1]. These do not necessarily invalidate the main findings, but they lower the quality of the study's reporting and should be considered when interpreting the results.

## In the end, how reliable are mandibular veneers?

This study does not show that mandibular veneers perform worse than maxillary ones. Their success rate was even reported higher at all three time points.

But these results are not enough to prove that mandibular veneers are superior either.

The more important point is that in both arches, more exposed dentin was associated with a greater need for intervention.

So in clinical decision-making, merely whether the arch is upper or lower should not be the main criterion for assessing risk. The amount of remaining enamel, the extent of the preparation and the share of exposed dentin remain very important.

Clinical message: a mandibular veneer is not necessarily a weaker or more complication-prone treatment; but preserving as much enamel as possible and limiting dentin exposure remain among the most important controllable factors for increasing treatment success.

value.title: Retrospective study of extensive heat-pressed ceramic veneers after 36 months
value.file_name: Retrospective study of extensive heat-pressed ceramic veneers after 36 months.pdf
value.key_finding: After 36 months, extensive heat-pressed ceramic veneers in a private practice had a 95.1% survival rate and 92.8% success rate, with ceramic fracture the main failure cause. Upper and lower jaw performed alike, while veneers with more than 50% exposed dentin needed significantly more interventions.
value.clinical_bottom_line: Extensive pressable ceramic veneers can be placed on mandibular as well as maxillary anterior teeth, but large exposed dentin areas raise the risk of recementation or endodontic intervention.
value.real_title: Retrospective study of extensive heat-pressed ceramic veneers after 36 months
value.journal: Journal of Esthetic and Restorative Dentistry
value.abstract: Statement of the Problem: The clinical performance of ceramic veneers is influenced by various clinical and material-related factors. Purpose: Retrospective evaluation of extensive anterior ceramic veneers in the upper and lower jaw 36 months after placement in a private practice. Materials and Methods: Thirty-seven patients (21 female, 16 male) were restored with adhesively luted extensive ceramic veneers made from a heat-pressed ceramic (Cergo, DeguDent, Hanau, Germany). One dentist restored a total of 130 teeth (maxilla N = 76, mandible N = 54). Adhesive cementation was performed with an etch-and-rinse adhesive (Optibond FL, Kerr Hawe, Karlsruhe, Germany) and a dual-curing composite cement. Results: After 36 months, the survival rate (in situ criteria) according to Kaplan-Meier was 95.1% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.88; 1). Reasons for failure were four ceramic fractures and one biological failure in five restored teeth. Of the restorations, 92.8% (95% CI: 0.86;1) were in service without any clinical intervention and rated successful after 36 months. Interventions were necessary in five cases (three recementations, two endodontic treatments). Clinical performance was not influenced by the veneer position (maxillar/mandibular, survival p = 0.3/success p = 0.4). Veneers with more than 50% of exposed dentin demonstrated a significantly increased risk (hazard ratio 10.6, p = 0.026) for a clinical intervention (recementation, endodontic treatment), whereas no effect on the survival rate could be detected (p = 0.17). Conclusions: After 36 months of clinical service, extensive veneer restorations made of a pressable ceramic showed a comparable survival and success rate in the upper and lower jaw. Large areas of exposed dentin (>50%) were associated with lower success rates. Clinical Significance: Mandibular ceramic veneers made using a heat-pressed ceramic offer the same clinical reliability as do veneers on anterior maxillary teeth. Dentin exposure significantly affects the clinical performance of heat-pressed ceramic veneers.

value.title: Retrospective evaluation of extended heat-pressed ceramic veneers after a mean observational period of 7 years
value.file_name: Retrospective evaluation of extended heat-pressed ceramic veneers after a mean observational period of 7 years.pdf
value.key_finding: After a mean of 7 years, extended heat-pressed glass-ceramic veneers had a 93.6% survival rate and 84.3% success rate, with ceramic fracture the main failure cause. Jaw position did not matter, but veneers on more than 50% exposed dentin needed significantly more clinical interventions.
value.clinical_bottom_line: Extended pressable veneers perform comparably in upper and lower anterior teeth, but dentin exposure above 50% of the preparation should be avoided or managed because it raises intervention risk.
value.real_title: Retrospective evaluation of extended heat-pressed ceramic veneers after a mean observational period of 7 years
value.journal: Journal of Esthetic and Restorative Dentistry
value.abstract: Objectives: Retrospective evaluation of extended anterior glass-ceramic veneers 7 years after placement in a private practice. Materials and Methods: A total of 31 patients (20 females/11 males) underwent restoration with adhesively luted extended veneers that were fabricated using heat-pressed glass-ceramic (Cergo, Dentsply Sirona). A single dentist restored 101 teeth (maxilla, n = 65; mandible, n = 36). Adhesive cementation was performed using an etch-and-rinse adhesive (OptibondFL, Kerr Corporation), and two different dual-curing composite cements (Variolink, Ivoclar Vivadent/Calibra, Dentsply Sirona). Results: After 7 years, the Kaplan-Meier survival rate (in situ criteria) was 93.6% (95% CI: 0.89; 0.98). The observed failures were caused by ceramic fractures for seven restorations and biological failure for one restoration. In total 80 of the 101 restorations were still in service and did not require any clinical intervention (7-year success rate: 84.3% [95% CI]: 0.76; 0.93). Interventions were necessary in 13 cases (8 recementations, 2 endodontic treatments, 2 composite fillings (caries), and 1 polishing of minor fractures). The clinical performance was not influenced by the veneer position (maxilla/mandible, survival P = .56/success P = .30). The veneers that covered large areas of exposed dentin (>50%) exhibited a significantly increased risk (hazard ratio 3.71, P = .0041) for requiring a clinical intervention; however, no effect on the survival rate was observed for these veneers (P = .35). Conclusions: Following 7 years of clinical service, extended anterior ceramic veneer restorations exhibited comparable survival and success rates for the upper and lower jaw. Large areas of exposed dentin (>50%) were associated with significantly lower success rates. Clinical Significance: Dentin exposure (more than 50% of the preparation surface) during preparation significantly affects the clinical performance of extended heat-pressed glass-ceramic veneers.

value.title: Retrospective evaluation of extended glass-ceramic ceramic laminate veneers after a mean observational period of 10 years
value.file_name: Retrospective evaluation of extended glass-ceramic ceramic laminate veneers after a mean observational period of 10 years.pdf
value.key_finding: After a mean of about 10 years, extended heat-pressed laminate veneers had a 91.8% survival rate and 78.6% success rate, with ceramic fracture the main failure cause and debonding the main complication. Mandibular and maxillary veneers performed alike, but veneers on more than 50% exposed dentin had a significantly higher intervention risk.
value.clinical_bottom_line: Extended veneers are a reasonable alternative to anterior full crowns, even in the mandible, but dentin exposure should be avoided or managed with different conditioning or luting strategies.
value.real_title: Retrospective evaluation of extended glass-ceramic ceramic laminate veneers after a mean observational period of 10 years
value.journal: Journal of Esthetic and Restorative Dentistry
value.abstract: Purpose: A retrospective evaluation of extended anterior ceramic laminate veneers (EACVs) after a mean observational period of 10 years. Methods: Thirty-one patients (20 females/11 males) underwent restoration with 101 adhesively luted, heat-pressed EACVs (maxilla, n = 65; mandible, n = 36). Results: The 10 year survival rate was 91.8% (95% confidence interval [95%-CI]: 0.87;0.97). Eight ceramic fractures, one biological failure, and one change in treatment plan caused the observed failures. Seventy-seven of the 101 restorations remained intervention-free in service (success rate: 78.6% [95%-CI: 0.70;0.88]). Fourteen interventions were needed (nine recementations, two endodontic treatments, two composite fillings, and one fracture polishing). The jaw position (maxilla/mandible, survival P = .578/success P = .056) had no influence on the clinical performance. EACVs covering large areas of exposed dentin (>50%) were associated with a significantly increased risk (hazard ratio 2.98, P = .019) of needing a clinical intervention (success rate: 68.0% [95%-CI: 0.52; 0.84]). However, the degree of dentin exposure had no effect on the survival rate (P = .761). Conclusions: After a mean observational period of 10 years, mandibular and maxillary EACVs exhibited survival and success rates that were comparable. Significantly lower success rates were associated with large areas of exposed dentin (>50%). Clinical Significance: Mandibular and maxillary EACV revealed 10-year survival rates comparable to those published for anterior metal-ceramic and glass-ceramic full-coverage crowns. Precaution should be taken not to expose dentin, and when large areas of dentin are exposed, different conditioning/luting strategies should be used.
